text: Victoria Manalo Draves (née Manalo; December 31, 1924 – April 11, 2010) was a Filipino American competitive diver who won gold medals in both platform and springboard diving at the 1948 Summer Olympics in London. She became the first woman to earn gold medals in both the ten-meter platform and three-meter springboard events and was the first American woman to win two gold medals in diving, as well as the first Asian American to win Olympic gold medals. Born in San Francisco’s South-of-Market district, she was the daughter of Philippine chef and musician Teofilo Manalo and English maid Gertrude Taylor, who met and married in San Francisco. She grew up with her parents, twin sister Connie, older sister Frankie, and younger brother Sonny, who died as a child. Unable to afford swimming lessons until age 10, she took summer lessons from the Red Cross, paying five cents for pool admission in the Mission District. She played badminton, basketball, and softball in high school and graduated from Commerce High School on Van Ness Avenue in 1942, working temporarily in the Army Port Surgeon's office to support her family. Introduced to diving at age 16 by Jack Lavery, she trained under Phil Patterson at the Fairmont Hotel Swimming and Diving Club, where racial discrimination led her to change her name to Vicki Taylor. Patterson’s military service during World War II caused her to pause diving, during which she worked at the Presidio military base. She later joined the Crystal Plunge in North Beach under coach Charlie Sava and trained with Jimmy Hughes, continuing her 50–100 dive after-school practices even while attending San Francisco Junior College (now City College of San Francisco). At 19, she finished third in her first national AAU diving competition at the Indiana meet in 1943. In 1944, she was befriended by Sammy Lee, who introduced her to Lyle Draves, who coached at the Athens Athletic Club in Oakland. Draves began training with Lyle Draves, adding platform diving to her springboard repertoire. After Lyle Draves left the San Francisco Bay Area due to racism at the Fairmont Hotel, she commuted to Los Angeles, placing second and third at the Outdoor Nationals. In 1945, following her father’s death, she returned to her job at the Army Port Surgeon's office in San Francisco. After the war, she moved permanently to Southern California, married Lyle Draves on July 12, 1946, and won the National Tower Diving Championship (10-meter platform) in 1946, 1947, and 1948. She won a total of five United States diving championships prior to the 1948 Olympics, despite not finishing first in either springboard or platform events at the Olympic trials in Detroit. On August 3, 1948, she won the springboard gold medal in London, followed by the 10-meter platform gold on August 6, becoming the first woman to win both titles. After her Olympic victory, she and her husband visited the Philippines, staying in a Malacañang Palace suite and visiting her father’s relatives in Orani, Bataan, where he was born. She gave platform diving exhibitions at Rizal Stadium and other venues, including for Philippine President Elpidio Quirino, and was named one of Life magazine’s top two U.S. athletes at the 1948 Olympics. After the Olympics, she turned professional, joining Larry Crosby’s “Rhapsody in Swimtime” aquatic show for her debut at Soldier Field in Chicago in 1948, and also performed at the L.A. Coliseum with Esther Williams and at the General Motors convention in Detroit. From 1949 to 1950, she toured the U.S., Canada, and Europe with Buster Crabbe’s “Aqua Parade.” After performing regularly at the El Mirador Hotel in Palm Springs and the Shadow Mountain Resort & Club in Palm Desert, she retired from diving. In the early 1950s, she started a family in Glendale and, with her husband, operated a swimming and diving training program at Indian Springs in Montrose, later moving it to Encino. They lived in Tarzana for 35 years, raising their four sons—David, Jeffery, Dale, and Kim—into skilled divers. Draves worked as a secretary while her husband remained a coach and swimming director. In the mid-1960s, she advocated for the Filipino Education Center as the second wave of Filipino immigrants settled in the South of Market district. In 1968, she joined Jesse Owens, Tommy Harmon, and Sam Hanks at the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas to raise $700,000 for the City of Hope National Medical Center. She was inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1969. In 2005, she was named the year’s Most Outstanding Alumnus of City College of San Francisco, receiving her award and speaking at the commencement ceremonies at the SF Masonic Auditorium, where she received a resounding ovation from the graduating students. That same year, she was recognized as one of Los Angeles Athletics Club’s outstanding athletes. In October 2006, a two-acre park in San Francisco—named Victoria Manalo Draves Park—was dedicated in her honor, located on Folsom and Sherman streets, the site of her former Franklin Elementary School, four blocks from where she was born and raised. Draves and her husband moved to Palm Springs, California in 1995. She died on April 11, 2010, aged 85, from pancreatic cancer aggravated by pneumonia. On August 3, 2020, she was honored with a Google Doodle in recognition of her achievements.
